newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower as US dlr climbs.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower as US dlr climbs.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended slightly lower Monday, giving back some early gains seen on news of a 300 tonne gold sale by the Dutch central bank in 1996, as the US dollar climbed to fresh 21-month highs against the German mark.

"Initially there was some relief that the bad news was out of the way for now, and that the gold market had managed to absorb both the Dutch central bank sale of about 10 million ounces and the hedging of 3.7 million ounces by Australia's Newcrest Mining," Chase Manhattan New York managing director Dinsa Mehta said.
"But the relief was tempered by the fear of more central bank sales to come," he said.
"Nevertheless, the market's ability to absorb so much gold makes claims that physical demand has been robust, by organizations like the World Council, look credible as a result now," he said.
"I'm not saying gold prices can't fall further, but it may be that the market currently offers reasonable value now," he said.
COMEX February gold ended down 50 cents at $359.70 an ounce, after seeing an intraday high at $361.70.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $358.30/70, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $359.60, and the New York close Friday at $358.80/30.

Earlier Monday the Dutch central bank said it sold 300 tonnes of gold, about one fifth of its reserves, raising $3.8 billion which it will hold as interest-bearing foreign currency reserves. The amount of gold sold by the Dutch is equivalent to about two thirds of South Africa's annual gold mine production.

"It looks like the Dutch sold the gold in the forward market in December, like they did in 1992 when they sold gold in November and December to a bullion bank which hedged it forward to February 93," CPM Group managing director Jeffrey Christian said.
"So the gold price may stay under pressure until the deliveries are out of the way," he said.
In 1992 the Dutch sold about 400 tonnes of gold and the Belgian central bank sold about 200 tones, which helped to drive the gold price down to $235 an ounce in early 1993.

In the first 10 days of 1997, spot gold had lost more than $13.00 an ounce or about 3.5 percent, posting new three year lows at $355.00, on fund selling, producer hedging and concern about European central bank gold sales.
Last week industry consultants Gold Fields Mineral Services issued a report saying central bank gold sales had accelerated in the second half of 1996.
However, earlier Monday Bundesbank president Tietmeyer also issued a statement saying G-10 countries had no intention "for the time being" of selling more gold.
But analysts fear increasing European central bank gold sales as the 1999 date for the introduction of a single European currency nears.
On Friday the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECI), unveiled a blueprint for management of monetary policy under the planned European monetary union.
"It looks like the Dutch may be building a war chest of foreign currency reserves to defend guilder in case the introduction of the euro currency fails," Christian said.
Gold found some strength against silver Monday, with the spot gold/silver ratio edging back up to 76.23 at the close, from 75.53 Friday, after sliding from 77.50 at the turn of the year.
COMEX March silver closed down 4.8 cents at $4.717 an ounce, after trading in a $4.795-4.675 intraday range.
Gold also regained some strength relative to platinum, with the April platinum/gold spread narrowing to $5.00 an ounce, from $6.00 Friday.
NYMEX April platinum ended down $2.10 at $366.70 an ounce, while NYMEX March palladium ended down 75 cents at $125.10.
